As of 315 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Heavy rain continues across southeastern portions of 
the area into this evening as a front lingers across the area.
Cooler, CAD conditions take hold for the remainder of the
forecast area.

This afternoon, high pressure is situated over Ontario, Canada 
extending over into New England and into northern portions of the 
Mid Atlantic. A nearly stationary front is draped across 
southeastern portions of the forecast area (roughly along the VA/NC 
border). Very heavy rain showers (and isolated storms) have 
developed along and just to the north of the boundary over Hampton 
Roads where multiple Flash Flood Warnings are in effect. Very 
efficient, warm rainfall processes, this afternoon thanks to flow off 
the warmer Atlantic/Chesapeake Bay waters combined with maximized 
PWATs of ~2+" over SE Virginia. We have seen rainfall rates of 5"+ 
per hour at times this afternoon with the current showers. 
Additional Flash Flood Warnings will likely be needed across 
portions of Hampton Roads/SE Virginia and potentially into NE North 
Carolina later this afternoon and evening as the activity continues 
to slide south. Rainfall rates should gradually lighten up later 
this evening into tonight as a cooler wedge airmass continues to 
push into the area from the north. It's a much different story for 
locations outside of SE VA/NE NC where we are seeing low clouds and 
mist/light showers, combined with much cooler temperatures in the 
60s to lower 70s due to the developing CAD wedge. Temperatures 
tonight will range from the mid 50s NW to around 70 SE. 

Additionally, northeast winds will increase throughout this evening 
and into tonight as the Canadian high pressure shifts east and low 
pressure forms off the NC/SC coast. Locations along the coast, 
including the entire Eastern Shore, Norfolk, Hampton Roads, and into 
Currituck County will see wind gusts upwards of 25 to 30 mph. The 
Atlantic coast of the Eastern Shore including Ocean City and 
Chincoteague will see their gusts build to 40 to 45 mph overnight. 
These higher gusts will persist for the coastline through Thursday 
night. Further inland, gusts to ~20mph are expected. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Strong onshore flow, cooler temperatures, and rainy 
conditions will continue on Wednesday. Rain chances gradually shift 
east Thursday, potentially making for a dry end to the week. Gusty 
winds will persist.

Cold air damming will overtake the area on Wednesday as high 
pressure remains parked to our north. This will make for our coolest 
day of the week as high temperatures top out in the low to mid 60s 
for the western and northern inland areas, with low 70s for the SE 
half of the CWA. It is possible that far NW portions of the area 
(Louisa) may stay in the upper 50s. Inland ~20 mph wind gusts are 
forecast through the day. Winds for coastal counties will 
persistently be blowing around 20 to 25mph with gusts to 35+ mph. 
The strongest winds will continue to be along the Atlantic coast 
with gusts to 40-45mph expanding down the span of our coastline 
through the day on Wednesday. These winds are forecast to stick 
around through Thursday night and even into Friday as the tightened 
pressure gradient between the strong high pressure to the north and 
the strengthening low pressure over the ocean remains. With the CAD 
wedge in place, the environment will be stable leading to mainly 
steady stratiform rain across the area on Wednesday and Thursday. 
Lows will cool off a few more degrees Wednesday night with low to 
mid 50s inland and low 60s east. 

Rain chances look to become more confined to eastern portions of the 
area Thursday into the first part of Friday as a secondary surface 
low forms along our coast and causes the main low to deepen, as well 
as finally have the potential to gain some forward momentum. Models 
still disagree on exactly where the low will be on Friday, with the 
GFS moving it off to the northeast while the ECMWF still keeps it 
closer to our shore. One solution will allow for winds to subside 
later Friday and drier air to move in for the weekend, while the 
other keeps the elevated impactful conditions lingering a bit 
longer. For now, the NBM solution is mostly a blend of the two 
solutions, keeping low-end rain chances lingering along the coast 
(especially NE) through the weekend. It is possible that the 
forecast may change substantially over the next few days for the 
weekend as we get more clarity on the placement of this coastal low. 

Highs on Thursday will still be well below normal as the 
effects of the CAD remain, with lower 60s forecast west of I-95 and 
upper 60s to lower 70s to the east. Thursday night will be rather 
chilly with far northwestern and western cool spots dipping into the
